newsitem.title: CROATIA: Hoping against hope, Serbs seek Croatian papers.
newsitem.headline: Hoping against hope, Serbs seek Croatian papers.

text.p: Cornered in a small enclave, minority Serbs are queuing up en masse to be citizens of a Croatian state they once repudiated with bloodshed.

More than 100,000 Serbs in Croatia's war-ravaged Eastern Slavonia region face reintegration under Croatian government authority after elections in April supervised by a U.N. transitional administration (UNTAES).

UNTAES has urged fearful Serbs to apply for Croatian citizenship papers to secure a future in a country with prosperous Western-oriented potential, rather than choose exile in impoverished socialist Serbia.

To that purpose, UNTAES has set up offices in 21 enclave towns where Croatian officials bussed in daily across ceasefire lines with a U.N. armoured escort process applications for personal identity papers including passports.
More than 40,000 Serbs so far have obtained the documents needed to vote, buy and sell property and get pensions and other social benefits, U.N. monitors in Vukovar say.
The experience of standing in line for documents emblazoned with the checkerboard symbol which they once equated with supposed Croatian fascism borders on traumatic for some Serbs.

For others, Croatian papers are just a practical insurance policy compensating for the failed promise of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to guarantee a breakaway Serb state carved by war out of newly independent Croatia in 1991.
All wonder whether the papers will mean much given the anti-Serb hostility of soon-to-return Croat neighbours that may be hard to restrain by the Zagreb government.
All things considered, however, Serbs are now flooding the documentation centres for varied reasons even as diehard compatriots stage daily street rallies against reintegration.
Most applicants for papers so far are middle-aged or elderly refugees seeking to reclaim or sell homes in the former rebel Krajina enclave reconquered in a 1995 Croatian offensive.
"We are all of us lost cases here, neither on heaven nor on earth. No one has decent accomodation and why should I not go back to my own home (in Krajina)," said an elderly woman.
Ilija Kalanj, 54, a worker from the old Krajina town of Benkovac but who now lives in Serbia, stood in the wan February sun gazing at new embossed family identity papers in his hand.

"These are the documents of my birthplace. I am very proud to have them. All I want is to go back where I was born. I am sure I could again live back there. The checkerboard does not bother me at all," he insisted.
Other applicants wanted only to sell property in order to build a new life in Serbia, however.

"I only want the papers so I can go back to Sibenik and see how they torched our home. Our father wants to sell what is left but later we will most probably move to Serbia," said Ruzica Popovic, a 22-year-old man.
Not many original Serb residents of Eastern Slavonia have come so far but they have more time to decide since they need only show up to collect pre-printed identity documents.

Dragoljub, a 55-year-old man dressed in his best but shabby suit, applied to be reunited with his Croat wife who evacuated her Croat mother to Zagreb during the 1991 war and was unable to return to rebel-held Vukovar.
"I just want the reintegration of my own family," he said.

Mirjana, a 42-year-old Vukovar woman, trembled nervously and dabbed her eyes as she signed her name on papers, submitted to fingerprinting and posed for a photograph. Her husband died fighting the Croats in 1991.

"This is a psychological trial for me and I'm not sure the doors will be so open to us once UNTAES is gone. I feel uncomfortable and ashamed. A lot of people like me are not telling their neighbours that they're coming here," she said.
U.N. troops and members of a transitional Serb-Croat police force guard all centres after attacks by Serb nationalist thugs aimed at intimidating applicants.
The Serb mayor of one town, Bobota, refused to provide space for a documentation centre. So U.N. administrator Jacques Klein, who lives in Bobota, set one up in his own garage.
